about.title: About this map and how it was made
sections: What this is

An interactive history of the land that is today Israel and the Palestinian territories, from 10,000 BCE to the present. Every number, date, border and name on the map comes from a source you can open, with a note on how it was checked.
How sure is each item?

Records are marked documented (directly recorded), estimated (a scholar’s reconstruction), contested (scholars or sides disagree; at least two sourced positions are given) or unknown (shown as unknown, never guessed). On the map, solid outlines are surveyed or legally defined boundaries, dashed outlines are approximate, soft dotted edges are schematic (the area is known, the edges are not) and hatching marks contested areas.
How territories before 1917 are drawn

Historians describe ancient extents in words: “Judea, Samaria and Galilee”. The map follows them, using 28 schematic regions bounded by rivers, wadis and coastlines. These regions are drawn by this project and are not historical borders; each territory says which regions it covered and which source describes it.
Claims and disputed status

Areas a state claims but does not govern are drawn as a dashed outline, not as control. Units held but whose status is internationally disputed (for example East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights since 1967, or the West Bank under Jordan in 1950–67) are hatched, and the panel names them.
Population

Figures are ranges as published, for a named area. Figures for different areas are not added together (for example, Israel’s and Palestine’s statistics bureaus both count East Jerusalem). The year panel shows the nearest published figures before and after the selected date; nothing is interpolated. Where scholars disagree, every estimate is shown. No absolute estimate exists before the Early Bronze Age, so none is shown.
Coastlines and the Dead Sea

Past coastlines and Dead Sea extents are models: published sea-level and lake-level reconstructions applied to an elevation model (SRTM on land, ETOPO1 offshore). They are schematic, especially offshore.
Names

Where communities use different names, all are shown with who uses them. Places are labelled with the name in use at the selected date; a switch shows today’s names instead. Names with no sourced date are treated as current usage and shown from 1800. A place destroyed or depopulated is drawn as a hollow ring only where the sources say it was not lived in again.
Colours

Colours come from colour-blind-safe palettes and avoid national flag colours and politically or religiously coded colours. Each modern colour choice is explained in the data so reviewers can challenge it.
Translations
English is the original. Arabic and Hebrew texts are machine-drafted unless marked reviewed, and carry a notice until a fluent reviewer has checked them.
Modern map layers

The 1947 partition plan, the 1949 armistice lines and demilitarised zones, the Oslo areas, the West Bank barrier, Israeli settlements by founding year and, for Gaza since 2023, schematic lines only. Each layer names its publisher, licence and date in the year panel. The 1947 plan is an approximate digitisation from the text of the UN resolution, because no open map of it exists.
Stories and perspectives

The guided tours and the perspectives page are written from the same sourced records: every sentence ends with a link to its source. Perspectives set out how Israeli, Palestinian and academic or international historians describe contested events, side by side, without declaring a winner.
What is not shown
Casualty figures for wars and attacks are deliberately left out at this stage.
Corrections and licences

All data is in plain files that anyone can review. The code is MIT-licensed and the project’s data CC BY 4.0, with short quotations remaining their authors’. Layers derived from OpenStreetMap are under the Open Database Licence (ODbL). Basemap: Natural Earth (public domain); elevation: SRTM, GMTED2010 and ETOPO1 (USGS, NOAA); place data: Wikidata (CC0) and Pleiades (CC BY).
